TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
MONDAY, 30 JANUARY 2023 AT 10:00 AM (AEST)
DAY 27
MR ANGUS SCOTT KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR TRENT GLOVER, for the Commonwealth

COMMISSIONER: Yes. And the appearances today?
MR SCOTT: May it please, Commissioner, I appear with Ms Marsh for today's proceeding.
COMMISSIONER: And, Ms Hogan-Doran, you've got Mr Glover?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Yes. I appear today with Mr Glover for the Commonwealth.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Mr Scott.
MR SCOTT: Commissioner, I call Annette Musolino.
COMMISSIONER: Now, Ms Musolino, will you take an oath or affirmation?
MS MUSOLINO: An affirmation, please, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Would you stand and I will just get that administered to you.
<ANNETTE LILLIAN MUSOLINO, AFFIRMED
<EXAMINATION BY MR SCOTT KC
COMMISSIONER: Thanks, Ms Musolino. Yes, Mr Scott.
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. Ms Musolino, would you please tell the Commission
your full name?
MS MUSOLINO: Annette Lillian Musolino.
MR SCOTT: And were you provided a Notice to Give a Statement and Produce Documents
from the Commission dated 7 October 2022?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And did you provide a response to that Notice with an annexure, called Annexure
A, dated 31 October 2022?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And were you provided a further Notice from the Commission dated 10
November 2022?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And have you provided these responses to that Notice, one dated 25 November

MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And another one - another response dated 29 November 2022?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And another response dated the 13th of December 2022?
MS MUSOLINO: I think my date is 11 December 2022.
MR SCOTT: Alright.
MS MUSOLINO: The annexure is 13 December 2022, but the Statement I have in my folder is
11 December 2022.
MR SCOTT: Perhaps if we bring it up on the screen.
MS MUSOLINO: Okay.
MR SCOTT: Do you see that on the screen, Ms -
MS MUSOLINO: I do. Yes, it's Statement 42.
MR SCOTT: Do you see the date of it?
MS MUSOLINO: I see 13 December. I just -
MR SCOTT: I've skipped over another Notice. That might explain the difference in the dates.
MS MUSOLINO: I apologise. I'm looking at Statement 107. Sorry. This is - yes. So this is the
third tranche of Statement 42. They're in a different order. I apologise. It's 13 December.
You're correct.
MR SCOTT: Thank you.
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And there was a Notice to you dated 1 December 2022; correct?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And a response from you dated the 11th of December - sorry, the 11th of January
2022?
MS MUSOLINO: Was that Statement 107? 107 was 11 December. I apologise. Counsel, could

MR SCOTT: It should be - perhaps if we get it up on the screen. Doc ID AMU.9999.0001.0007.
Do you see that?
COMMISSIONER: In my index, it's shown as an answer to 107 and it's 11th of December 2022.
MR SCOTT: Yes. So that's the correct -
MS HOGAN-DORAN: That's - Commissioner, that's my line as well.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Thank you, Commissioner. Are your various Statements true and
correct to the best of your knowledge and belief, Ms Musolino?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, just before my friend continues and leads from this, can
I just confirm with him that he dealt with the Statement of 6 November which includes a
revised Annexure A. I know he dealt with the Annexure A dated 31 October 2022, but there
is a revised - I'm instructed there's a revised version of that annexure dated 6 November.
MR SCOTT: I didn't deal with that. Ms Musolino, was there a revised Annexure A of the date
your Counsel just identified?
MS MUSOLINO: There was, yes.
MR SCOTT: Yes. Thank you.
COMMISSIONER: Do you have a document number for that, Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: I don't presently, Commissioner, but I will have it attended to. And if
there's any difficulty with the material - a disconnect between the exhibit list and what I'm
instructed, I will take that up between the Commonwealth and those instructing Mr Scott.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR SCOTT: It doesn't appear on the exhibit list at present, Commissioner. We will need to
address that in the course of today's proceedings.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MR SCOTT: But in the meantime, Commissioner, I tender the documents on the exhibit listed
for today's proceedings, with the exception of those documents highlighted in red which are
already exhibits.

MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, can I just - on that note, Exhibit 4209, although on the
exhibit list it is identified as 31 October, I'm instructed that the exhibit ending in 0001 is the 6
November version of the annexure. So, the exhibit number is the correct number; it's just the
date of 31 October is incorrect.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. So we've got everything we need?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: You do.
COMMISSIONER: It's just the list is a bit wrong, saying the date is 31 October when it should
be 6 November. Thanks for that, Ms Hogan-Doran. You're happy with that?
MR SCOTT: I am. I'm indebted to my friend.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. So 4207 through to 4303 are admitted, each of the documents
identified in the exhibit list, with the numbers they are given in the list.
<EXHBITS 4207 TO 4303 TENDERED AS PER THE EXHIBIT LIST
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. Now, Ms Musolino, it's correct, isn't it, that you
commenced your employment with the Department of Human Services in October 2012?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Prior to that, you occupied various roles, your first job as a solicitor being in 1994
at a firm called Snedden Hall & Gallop; correct?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: You were admitted as a solicitor in 1993; correct?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And in that first year, working in that firm, your key responsibilities included
assisting with matters involving commercial litigation, debt recovery, bankruptcy and
insolvency, as well as employment and criminal law; correct?
MS MUSOLINO: Correct.
MR SCOTT: And may we take it from that that you are familiar with the requirements of
proof of debt in legal proceedings?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: You hold a current practising certificate?

MR SCOTT: Your current role is not a legal position; correct?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Is this right: you're presently Chief Operating Officer within Services Australia?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. And is this right: you haven't held a legal role since you were Chief
Counsel of the Department of Human Services between 7 April 2015 and 6 January 2019?
MS MUSOLINO: That's correct.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. During your time as Chief Counsel for that Department during that
period - is this right - you, from time to time, acted in non-legal roles, including acting as
Chief Operating Officer and Deputy Secretary within the Enabling Services area of the
Department?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes. They weren't - those titles weren't consistent across the period when I
acted. They were sometimes Deputy Secretary or Deputy CEO roles, as opposed to Chief
Operating Officer. So there were variations in title. There was also a period that I acted in a
business role in the WPIT Program. But otherwise, yes, that's correct.
MR SCOTT: The WPIT Program being?
MS MUSOLINO: The Welfare Payment Infrastructure Transformation Program, which was a
business transformation - a business-led transformation of the IT and legacy systems.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Is this right: during the period that we are describing, the Legal Services
division, of which you were responsible as Chief Counsel, included various areas - various
branches, I should say, including the Freedom of Information and Litigation Branch?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Also known as FoIL?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And from around October 2016 during your tenure as Chief Counsel, one of the
branches in the LSD was the Ombudsman and Information Release Branch; correct?
MS MUSOLINO: I will just check. Yes, I think that's correct.
MR SCOTT: Thank you.

MR SCOTT: Thank you. That branch was headed by a non-legal SES with the title of National
Manager; correct?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And from 17 October 2016 to 31 July 2018, that role was occupied by someone
called Michael Robinson?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. You deal, Ms Musolino, at paragraph 23 of your first Statement of
circumstances in which matters might be escalated to you. Do you agree with me on that?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: By way of "escalated to you", what are you referring?
MS MUSOLINO: So what I mean is in the context of a large legal division with six practice
teams - practice areas and six teams, from time to time there would be a matter that had a
particular significance or sensitivity that needed the attention of the Chief Counsel and
potentially the attention of the Executive. So "escalation" means bringing it to my attention.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Would - and that would include circumstances relating to AAT1
matters where there was particular sensitivity and significance; correct?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: For example, would this type of matter fall within a category that you would
expect in the usual course to be escalated to you, namely, a Tier 1 AAT decision identifying
that a fundamental aspect of the Scheme administered by the Department was contrary to
law?
MS MUSOLINO: It would depend on the exact terms of the AAT decision. But if the
determination was that that's what it represented, I would expect that to be escalated.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. So, for example, in the context of the Robodebt Scheme, a decision of
the AAT at Tier 1 indicating that the use of averaging as it was being used in that Scheme was
unlawful, would you expect that to be escalated to you in the usual course?
MS MUSOLINO: If that's what it concluded, as opposed to if it concluded that averaging was
not available in a particular matter, which I wouldn't expect to be escalated to me.
MR SCOTT: Okay. At paragraph 115 of your first Statement, you describe your role as Chief
Counsel, including:

...oversight of the legal team that acted on behalf the DSS Secretary in legal proceedings that
related to the Robodebt Scheme.
Do you see that?
MS MUSOLINO: I see that, yes.
MR SCOTT: And when you say - referring to DSS Secretary - sorry, the legal team acting on
behalf of the DSS Secretary, is this right: that primary statutory responsibility, or the
decisions the subject of AAT review, was vested in the DSS Secretary; correct?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: But that the practical administration of those matters were effectively delegated
to the Department of Human Services; correct?
MS MUSOLINO: Effectively, yes, because we were a service provider. We were effectively in
the role of service provider to the Department of Social Services in undertaking those AAT
matters.
MR SCOTT: And one aspect of providing those services was providing a legal team to act on
behalf of the DSS Secretary in those legal proceedings?
MS MUSOLINO: In the AAT - well, in the AAT2, yes. In the AAT1, the Secretary of the
Department of Social Services did not appear. And so it was more limited role. There could
be requests from the AAT for submissions, but the Department's involvement in AAT1
matters extended to the provision of T docs - what are called T docs to assist the
Commission, and they were the documents relevant to the matter. And that work was
handled in the Integrity and Information Group, I think in the Appeals area.
MR SCOTT: One area relevant to AAT1 matters that fell within your Division was providing
advice on prospects of appeal from AAT Tier 1 decisions to AAT Tier 2; correct?
MS MUSOLINO: There was a team within the Litigation Branch, correct, that did what were
called a further administrative review. Their role was to review every AAT1 decision that had
a less favourable outcome for the Secretary of the Department of Social Services to
determine if they would recommend an appeal. And they would make that assessment
against the standing operational statements and litigation principles established by the
Department of Social Services.
MR SCOTT: Yes. And that advice that you are describing, that they were provided, is also
known as an AFAR?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And the effect of it would be that the advice would be provided and then

MS MUSOLINO: I think, yes, the way it worked is if an appeal was recommended, that would
be sent to the Department of Social Services for a decision. If no appeal was recommended, I
don't think it went to the Department of Social Services.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And in respect of your role, which you described as oversight of that legal
team, would you agree that role included oversight of that team's compliance with model
litigant principles?
MS MUSOLINO: It - my role involved making sure we had systems in place across the Legal
Division to comply with the model litigant principles. I didn't supervise that team. That was a
team that sat within a Branch which reported to a General Counsel who did the day-to-day
supervision. But the way I would describe my obligation was to make sure there were
systems in place, such as training, guidance material, continuing legal education and systems
for escalation of allegations of model litigant. So that would be my role.
MR SCOTT: Yes. And that General Counsel would have reported to you?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. And would your role also include oversight in the sense you've
described with respect to ethical conduct relating to those proceedings?
MS MUSOLINO: Again, that would be - my role would be to make sure there were processes
in place and systems. So I would describe my role more as a manager of the legal team,
managing the resources and the training and the systems and the processes, rather than the
day-to-day supervision. So it would have been about having systems in place to make sure
that they were conducted ethically and appropriately - systems and training and escalation
where required.
MR SCOTT: If it came to your attention that there was a contravention of the model litigant
principles or the ethical obligations that were relevant, you would take action; correct?
MS MUSOLINO: There was a process - so where any - from time to time, there would be an
allegation of a breach of model litigant, we had a process in place for that to be considered in
terms of what action needed to be taken and to be escalated. If it needed to be reported, it
had to be reported to the - to the Office of Legal Services Coordination for their
consideration. So we did have a system in place so that where there was an allegation or
a - of a breach of model litigant, that could be dealt with.
MR SCOTT: Right. And were you responsible for ensuring that process was followed?
MS MUSOLINO: I would say - I was responsible for having the system in place and for - where
I became - if I became aware it wasn't being followed, taking action if that - if that was
training or discipline or whatever it would be. If I was aware that it wasn't being followed,
then I would have taken action.

MR SCOTT: And would the same apply for contravention of ethical obligations of a solicitor
within your Division?
MS MUSOLINO: The same would apply - and it would also be considered in terms of the APS
Code of Conduct if that was the issue. It might be - if there was a breach of some obligation,
it would be referred for consideration under the Code of Conduct.
MR SCOTT: You were - prior to being Chief Counsel in a permanent capacity, you acted in the
role of Chief Counsel from 1 June 2014 to 4 January 2015; correct?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Can the witness please be shown - before I go on, I've neglected to
identify - you've got a number of folders there in front of you, Ms Musolino. Can I just ask
you to identify what those folders are?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes. So it's exhibit - it's volume 1. This is what I was given - the Hearing Block
3, volume 1 of 2 draft exhibits.
MR SCOTT: Okay.
MS MUSOLINO: And then volume 2 of 2 draft exhibits. And the AAT bundle exhibits. And this
morning I was given the further draft exhibits. And I have a chronology of key events that I'm
using as well.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Chronology of key events: what's the nature of that?
MS MUSOLINO: It's a document that just reminds me where - I was in a multitude of jobs. It's
just a reminder of what jobs I was in at various points.
MR SCOTT: Okay. An aide-memoire, as it were?
MS MUSOLINO: It is, yes.
MR SCOTT: Commissioner, does - do you have a view on whether that should be tendered,
that aide-memoire?
COMMISSIONER: Sorry. Say that again, whether the aide-memoire should be tendered?
MR SCOTT: The aide-memoire.
COMMISSIONER: Well, at present I don't see any particular reason, but if it occurs to you
that it ought to -?
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner.

COMMISSIONER: Would it be of assistance to the Commission to see where you were when,
do you think, Ms Musolino?
MS MUSOLINO: I think it just reflects what's in my Statement, Commissioner, just because
it's over a long period of time.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Thank you.
MR SCOTT: I'm content with that, Commissioner. Alright. Can the witness please be shown
Exhibit 4223, Doc ID CTH.3008.0006.5274, which hopefully is your tab 22, Ms Musolino, of
your first volume.
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Do you have that? Ms Musolino, do you have that?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes. Sorry. Yes.
MR SCOTT: Do you agree with me that is an email from yourself to Mr Hutson, indicating
your intention to apply for the role of Chief Counsel, dated 3 November 2014?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes, it's my application. It's the cover email to the actual application.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. And could the witness please be shown what should be your tab 24,
Ms Musolino, Exhibit 4225, Doc ID CTH.3008.0006.5280. Do you have that?
MS MUSOLINO: I have that, yes.
MR SCOTT: Do you accept that this was part of the documents you submitted with your
application by that email?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Is this what in Public Service speak is normally called a Selection Criteria
Statement?
MS MUSOLINO: A Response to Selection Criteria. Yes.
MR SCOTT: Yes. And, in effect, what you seek to do is address the various criteria for
selection for the job that you're applying for; correct?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And, for example, at the top of that first page of the document, the heading is
‘Shape Strategic Thinking’. Do you see that?

MR SCOTT: Is ‘Shape Strategic Thinking’ one of the selection criteria that you had to address
for the application?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Alright. I'm just going to ask you about the first paragraph under that
heading, which is:
From 2015, the Department must meet an ambitious service delivery agenda in line with
government priorities in a challenging Budget environment. In the Legal Services Division, this
will require strategic focus to properly balance continuous efficiency improvements, with the
need to deliver on key priorities.
Ms Musolino, did you have an understanding as at the date of your application submitted at
the end of 2014 that there was an ambitious service delivery agenda that was proposed for
the following year?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Did you have an understanding that agenda included what later became the
Robodebt Scheme?
MS MUSOLINO: No.
MR SCOTT: What were you referring to in terms of the ambitious service delivery agenda?
MS MUSOLINO: It's a fairly broad expression of what I understood was happening in the
Department of Human Services. So if I can provide a bit of context, Commissioner. The
Department only became a department around 2010, 2011, when it brought together
Centrelink, Medicare and Child Support. That was a huge change. It brought together
different teams who were working on different programs and different systems and different
processes, different employment conditions. So the Department pretty much from then had
been on a transformation to become, you know, one joined-up service delivery agency.
So this is a very broad description of all the activity that was going on. It reflects probably an
understanding that WPIT was underway - the WPIT program, which was a huge
transformation program. I don't believe I was referring to any particular program. It was
actually the fact that we knew we had legacy systems that needed reform. We needed to
streamline our processes. We needed to get our staff working across programs. So it was a
massive service delivery agenda to transform the way we service the Australian public.
COMMISSIONER: Can I just ask you about the legal systems that needed reform. What are
you referring to there?
MS MUSOLINO: In terms of the legal team, Commissioner?

COMMISSIONER: Well, I'm asking you. You said that, "We had legal systems that needed
reform.” I'm just asking what you're referring to.
MS MUSOLINO: No, I may have mis-spoke. So we needed - so systems and processes across -
COMMISSIONER: I may have misheard you. You may have said "legacy systems".
MS MUSOLINO: "Legacy". I apologise. Yes.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Alright.
MS MUSOLINO: So I'm thinking of IT systems that don't talk to each other, that are, you
know, not always entirely reliable. I'm thinking of - I mean, one of the big challenges was
staff who were used to working in one program rather than working across Medicare,
Centrelink, Child Support. And also, how we thought about service delivery. So thinking
about the customer or the recipient or the parent in the case of Child Support. But thinking
about them in a unified way rather than just in a transactional way around the program. So
what I meant - what I intended, I think, was to say we've got a lot of work to be getting on
with, a lot of service delivery. And there had been projects already, when I joined, around
service delivery reform. I think that's what they were called, service delivery reform. So it
was just aligned to that, I think.
COMMISSIONER: And now I'm interested in what you say about thinking about recipients in a
unified way rather than just around a program. Robodebt seemed to have been the opposite
of that, but do you want to comment on that?
MS MUSOLINO: I think I would like to comment on that, Commissioner. What I - I made the
point at the beginning that we had only - the Department had only really become a
department around 2010, 2011. It was very much on a journey of maturing. So it - I would
say when I joined in 2012, it didn't particularly have great maturity around how it dealt with
risk, how it thought about the customer or the recipient. That was all still forming. And one
of the issues was the business was quite - the businesses were quite siloed.
So we had service delivery occurring here at the front, but not always with a - with an
appreciation or a planning around the down-river impact. So if you did something - you
know, just use a simple example. If - when a customer was granted a payment and that was
all established, if that wasn't done properly and the customer didn't understand their
obligations or we hadn't captured their information, there would be a down-river impact for
the customer. It might be a debt. It might be a cancellation of payment. There wasn't always
a joined-up end-to-end consideration of how we were dealing with the individual.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. I understand what you're saying. I will be interested to hear later
on, perhaps, about how Robodebt presented any different process and how those problems
were overcome, if they were at all. But I will just let Mr Scott go on for the moment. Thanks
for that.

MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. Can we take it from that first paragraph, the specific
identification in it of the imperative for the Department to meet an ambitious service
delivery agenda and the role that the Legal Services Division would play in it, that you were
seeking to represent to - in this job application, that by being appointed to the role of
General Counsel, you could assist with ensuring the Legal Services Division contributes to
meeting that agenda?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. If we call out, please, the third paragraph on that page. Do you see
there that third paragraph says:
The Department's delivery of payments and services within a complex, legal and political
environment gives rise to significant challenges and opportunities.
And you say:
My approach is to identify the desired outcome and develop a road map to achieve it.
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: I'm interested in that last sentence:
My approach is to identify the desired outcome and develop a road map to achieve it.
Can you explain what that means?
MS MUSOLINO: So what I'm trying to reflect there is a really good legal team will actually be
involved in matters from the get-go in helping to - you know - and will help design processes
so that they can actually achieve whatever outcome, you know, the business wants lawfully.
But, ideally, you're at the table at the beginning of the design of a process and you are
helping to map it so that there - you know, the opposite of that, which I've certainly
experienced in other places - and, actually, I would say probably there was an element of this
when I joined the Department of Human Services - is at the very last minute, Legal is brought
in as a rubber stamp to something that has already been built, planned. So what I'm trying to
indicate there is my approach is be at the table, understand what they are trying to achieve
and find a lawful way through the complexity to achieve the outcome.
MR SCOTT: Okay. If we go to the third page of the document, please, and call out paragraph
2. It states:
I believe there are core non-negligible behaviours for APS officers.
And one of those that you identify is dealing honestly -
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.

MR SCOTT: - with staff, management and stakeholders?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Alright. And do you adhere to those values?
MS MUSOLINO: I do, and I believe I have always adhered to those values in my career.
MR SCOTT: Okay. If we go to page 6, please. Do you accept that in the first paragraph on that
page, you refer to your admission as a legal practitioner in the High Court and the Supreme
Court in the ACT and in New South Wales?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And you refer to having, at that time, an unrestricted ACT practising certificate?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And you refer then in the next paragraph to having undertaken a range of
different and challenging legal roles and having broad experience in various legal areas,
including administrative law, with particular expertise in relation to Freedom of Information
and privacy law. Do you see that?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Now, as a lawyer, you would - is this right - have an understanding of the
significant disciplinary consequences of misrepresenting your skills and experience in a
document such as this?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And may we take it that where you have represented your skills and experience
in this document, you have carefully considered those representations to ensure that they
are accurate?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And so when you have represented in this document that you had broad
experience in various legal areas, including administrative law, we can take it, can we, that is
a true statement?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes, it's - with the proviso that it's - I made the point that it's particular
expertise. So it's broad experience, and the particular expertise is in relation to Freedom of
Information, which I spent a significant amount of time doing in the Department of
Education, Employment and Workplace Relations, and privacy law, which I had pretty much
practised in for most of my career.

MR SCOTT: Okay. Can we call out the next - paragraph 6, please. The same page. Do you see
there, the first sentence, you refer to a deep understanding of Freedom of Information law.
Do you see that?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes.
MR SCOTT: But in the next sentence, you identify as an additional area that you also have a
thorough understanding of administrative law principles. Do you see that?
MS MUSOLINO: Yes. But I think that statement relates to the Freedom of Information law.
And it's evident from my CV that that's what I had experience in.
MR SCOTT: Well, I suggest to you that you're clearly seeking to represent that you have a
thorough understanding of administrative law principles beyond merely Freedom of
Information law.
MS MUSOLINO: Well, I would have had an understanding of administrative law principles. I
had been to university. I had done admin law at uni. I had worked at ASIC for a period and
understood administrative law principles there. But the reason I put it as a subparagraph
following the reference to Freedom of Information law is that's what I'm trying to draw to
the attention of the committee.
MR SCOTT: Well, of course, the role of General Counsel is not limited to Freedom of
Information law, is it?
MS MUSOLINO: It's actually very, very broad. So there were some areas that I had more
experience in than others. FOI and privacy, commercial law, contractual matters, they were
the areas that I had more of an expertise in. It's not confined to FOI, but Freedom of
Information was an extremely large part of the Department of Human Services legal work.
We receive many, many thousands of FOI requests a year, as well as hundreds of thousands
of information requests. So information and privacy law was a key component of the work of
the Legal Division.
MR SCOTT: As someone that had been in government legal practice for some time by the
time of this statement, you would have understood that a significant aspect of administrative
law are the principles relating to the lawfulness of administrative decision-making, wouldn't
you?
MS MUSOLINO: And I would have been aware of those principles.
MR SCOTT: Right. And I suggest to you that you're representing in this document that you
have a thorough understanding of those principles.
MS MUSOLINO: I think I had a thorough understanding of admin law principles as they
related to Freedom of Information law, but I also had an understanding of administrative law
principles more generally.

MR SCOTT: To the extent that there were limitations on your knowledge of administrative
law principles relating to the lawfulness of administrative decision-making, would you agree
with me that the existence of those limitations would be a significant reason why you would
defer to the opinions of other legal practitioners with greater experience in that area than
you?
MS MUSOLINO: It's a rather long question. I might see if I can answer it. I - as Chief Counsel, I
was not a subject matter expert in every area of practice, or in any of them, I would say. I
